children: Talen Energy's latest deal is a win-win for the power producer: It now has guaranteed revenue sources for the next decade, but can still take advantage of rising electricity prices.

The power producer said Wednesday it signed a seven-year agreement to provide 750 megawatts of generating capacity from its Guernsey Power Station in Guernsey County, Ohio, to an "investment-grade counterparty." The deal is expected to generate about $100 million in annual revenue, beginning with the 2029-2030 delivery year.
Combined with revenue from the company's previous agreements, the new deal is expected to generate roughly $1 billion in cumulative revenue over the next 10 years, according to a news release.
Shares of Talen jumped 4.1% to $377.29 Wednesday, putting the stock on pace for its highest close since hitting $400.12 on July 15, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
Evercore ISI analysts said the deal strengthens Talen's investment case by making its earnings more predictable, without limiting how much the company can benefit from higher electricity prices.

The analysts estimate the agreement implies a capacity price of about $365 per megawatt per day — that's roughly 8% higher than what Talen could receive through an upcoming regional capacity auction, which covers power plants across the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic.

An agreement reduces Talen's reliance on such auctions, which can subject power producers to unpredictable pricing, according to the analysts. By securing long-term payments, Talen can generate more consistent revenue while maintaining the opportunity to profit from higher electricity prices.

It also builds on Talen's efforts to secure longer-term contracts, including its existing deal with Amazon Web Services. Together, those arrangements increase the share of Talen's gross margin under contract to 40% through 2036.

Talen's announcement comes as power stocks have started rebounding after months of weakness. Investors appear to be encouraged by signs that electricity producers can still capitalize on booming demand from artificial data centers, while navigating growing political opposition to their development.
